text: The share of people in extreme poverty fell from nearly 40% in 1990 to under 10% by 2019 — then stalled as COVID-19, conflict, and climate disruption reversed progress in many regions
More than 90% of people in extreme poverty live in sub-Saharan Africa or South Asia — in some countries more than half the population lives below the $2.15-a-day line
In the Democratic Republic of Congo, over 75% of the population lives in extreme poverty — one of the highest rates anywhere in the world
The average person in the world's 10 richest countries earns roughly 50 times more than the average person in the 10 poorest — a gap that has barely narrowed in decades
The global average income is pulled up dramatically by a small number of very wealthy countries — the typical person on Earth earns far less than the average suggests
Luxembourg's GDP per capita exceeds $120,000 per year; Burundi's is under $300 — a 400-fold gap that illustrates how little the global average tells you about any individual country
Wealth inequality is far more extreme than income inequality — owning assets (property, shares) compounds advantage over time in a way that wages alone do not
Wealth inequality worsened after the 2008 financial crisis as stock and property prices recovered faster than wages, benefiting those who already owned assets
North America and Europe together hold more than 60% of all global household wealth, despite containing less than 20% of the world's population
